findings.claim: Goat's milk fats carry the fatty acids that give the lemony, goaty tang.
findings.because: The goat fatty acids (caproic, caprylic, capric) give the goaty, animal note. The lemony tang comes from lactic acid made by the cultures. The sentence gives both to the fat, which contradicts the card's own trap why.
findings.fix: Goat's milk fatty acids give the goaty note. Cultures give the tang.

findings.claim: The English name for Parmigiano-Reggiano, from Parma and Reggio Emilia
findings.because: Outside the EU, and above all in the US, 'parmesan' is a generic name. Domestic parmesan is legally aged only about 10 months and made in other ways. A server who treats the two as the same name will promise a guest Italian, year-aged, calf-rennet cheese that the kitchen may not be using. The PDO zone also covers Modena and parts of Bologna and Mantua.
findings.fix: English for Parmigiano-Reggiano, though US parmesan can be domestic

findings.claim: made around Parma from raw, part-skimmed cow's milk and aged 12 to 36 months
findings.because: Twelve months is the legal minimum. Wheels are commonly sold at 40, 48 or even 72 months or more, so 36 is not a ceiling.
findings.fix: made around Parma from raw, part-skimmed cow's milk and aged 12 months or far longer

findings.claim: This is smooth, tangy and set cold.
findings.because: Fromage blanc is cultured at room temperature, roughly 20 to 30 C (68 to 86 F), not in the cold. The real contrast with ricotta is that it is set by cultures without being heated.
findings.fix: This is smooth, tangy and set without heat.

findings.claim: Butter cooked until its milk solids toast and smell of nuts
findings.because: Ghee is also butter cooked until its milk solids toast and smell nutty, and Ghee is on this section's roster. As a test option this gist would be accepted for both. What makes this one this one is that the browned solids stay in the butter, where ghee strains them out.
findings.fix: Butter cooked until its milk solids brown, kept in for a nutty taste

findings.claim: Pure butterfat with the water and milk solids taken out
findings.because: This also describes Ghee, which is on this section's roster, so the two gists could be swapped in the test. The thing that sets this one apart is that the solids come out before they brown, so the fat stays pale and mild.
findings.fix: Pale, mild butterfat, milk solids lifted off before they brown

findings.claim: It's what makes our biscuits tender and the fried chicken so juicy.
findings.because: The card is generic, but this line tells the server to claim dishes the house may not serve. A new hire will repeat it word for word at a table where there are no biscuits.
findings.fix: It's the classic secret to tender biscuits and juicy fried chicken.

findings.claim: It softens into anything warm, like the beets here.
findings.because: It points at a dish ('the beets here') that the guest may not have ordered and the menu may not have. Roasted beets with goat cheese are also often served cold. The line also almost repeats the crème fraîche guest line ('It melts into anything warm').
findings.fix: It's lovely with beets, honey or a warm salad.

findings.claim: It's a hard Italian cheese aged at least a year
findings.because: 'At least a year' only holds for true Parmigiano-Reggiano. A guest who asks about 'parmesan' on an American menu may be getting a domestic or generic parmesan, which can be aged less and need not be Italian. A server should not promise the age.
findings.fix: It's a hard, long-aged Italian cheese, nutty and savory with little crunchy crystals.

findings.claim: rich enough to boil
findings.because: 'Rich enough to boil' is kitchen shorthand. A new hire will not see that it means 'will not curdle when heated', so it does not help them tell this option apart.
findings.fix: Thick cultured cream, mildly tangy, that won't curdle when heated

findings.claim: Rich, warm and deeply savory.
findings.because: It is a verbless fragment that sounds read off a card. 'Deeply savory' also oversells. Brown butter is nutty and toasty, and the line has already said hazelnuts.
findings.fix: It's rich and warm.

findings.claim: Pure butterfat with the water and milk solids taken out
findings.because: Clarified butter is still butter. Trace milk proteins remain after clarifying, and it is not a substitute for a guest who avoids milk. A server who repeats 'milk solids taken out' can sound like they are promising the butter has no milk left in it.
findings.fix: Butterfat with most of the water and milk solids cooked off

findings.claim: It's butter melted down to just the pure golden fat.
findings.because: 'Just the pure golden fat' tells a guest nothing else is left. Traces of milk protein remain, so this can be heard as an assurance to someone who avoids dairy.
findings.fix: It's butter melted down to its golden fat, the milky bits skimmed off.

findings.claim: It's what makes our biscuits tender and the fried chicken so juicy.
findings.because: This states what this kitchen's dishes are made with. The server has not checked the recipe and recipes vary. Ingredient claims belong only in madeWith, which comes with 'Confirm with the kitchen.'
findings.fix: It's a tangy, lightly thick cultured milk, the classic for tender biscuits and juicy fried chicken.

findings.claim: The classic is made from butter alone.
findings.because: The guest line says it 'smells like hazelnuts', so a guest with a nut allergy will ask. A server who learned 'butter alone' will pass it on as a promise, but some kitchens finish brown butter with nuts. The card should say where the name comes from and stop there.
findings.fix: The name comes from its color and smell, not from nuts in it.

findings.claim: Fior di Latte
findings.because: Fior di latte means cow's-milk mozzarella specifically. The buffalo version is a different cheese, mozzarella di bufala. With this alias on the card, 'sometimes buffalo milk' in madeWith contradicts the card's own name, and a server could call buffalo mozzarella fior di latte.
findings.fix: Drop 'sometimes buffalo milk' from madeWith and keep the alias, or keep the buffalo line and drop the alias

findings.claim: butterfat-fluency-butter-cream-and-cultures
findings.because: That entry is a broad survey of butter, cream and cultured dairy that mentions ghee in one clause. It is not the long-form essay on ghee, and the rule allows a lexiconSlug only when the entry covers this same subject.
findings.fix: Omit lexiconSlug

findings.claim: Pierced so an edible mold veins the paste, sharp, salty and creamy
findings.because: As an answer option it opens on a verb with no subject, and "paste" is cheesemonger jargon for the interior that a new hire will not know. The option is hard to parse at a glance.
findings.fix: Wheel pierced so an edible mold grows in veins, sharp, salty, creamy

findings.claim: It's butter whipped with herbs and garlic, then chilled.
findings.because: The guest line tells the guest this butter holds garlic, but the flavorings change from kitchen to kitchen. The card's own madeWith lists garlic only as "often", and many are citrus, anchovy or blue cheese butters. A server repeating this line would be making a promise about the plate.
findings.fix: It's butter mixed with herbs and seasonings, then chilled.

findings.claim: then strained, so all that's left is pure, rich butter flavor
findings.because: Saying the solids are strained off and only 'pure' butter is left sounds like the milk is gone. A guest avoiding milk could take it as clearance. Straining leaves traces of milk protein and lactose behind, and ghee is still a dairy product.
findings.fix: It's butter cooked slowly until golden and nutty, then strained, for a rich, toasty butter flavor you can't get from plain butter.

findings.claim: then strained off
findings.because: The line says the milk solids are 'strained off' and nothing says the result is still butter from milk. Next to the guest line, a server could say the milk part has been removed. Traces stay, and the madeWith list shows only 'butter'.
findings.fix: Butter simmered until its milk solids toast golden, then strained out

findings.claim: so an edible mold veins the paste
findings.because: 'Edible' tells the guest the mold is safe to eat, and a server will repeat it. That is an assurance, not a description. Some guests with a penicillin allergy ask about Penicillium cheeses, and the card should describe the mold without judging it.
findings.fix: Pierced so a mold culture veins the paste, sharp, salty and creamy

findings.claim: Inside it's much milder, soft, savory and a little meaty.
findings.because: Washed rind covers semi-firm and firm cheeses too: Raclette, Appenzeller, Gruyère and Comté are brine-washed or smear-ripened. Only some are soft, such as Taleggio, Epoisses and Munster, so a server who says every one is soft will be wrong at the table.
findings.fix: Inside it's much milder, often soft, savory and a little meaty.

findings.claim: It's rubbed with brine as it ages, so the rind turns orange and smells bold.
findings.because: The guest asked what it is, and the line never says it is a cheese or gives an example. It opens on the process, so a nervous server answering at the table sounds like they skipped the answer. The partner card fd_0170 names Brie and Camembert. Taleggio is the washed rind a guest is most likely to know.
findings.fix: It's a cheese like Taleggio, rubbed with brine as it ages, so the rind turns orange and smells bold.

findings.claim: A firm, chalky center means it is young, not spoiled.
findings.because: "Not spoiled" is a condition assurance a server would repeat about a specific wheel. The true fact is that a chalky center is normal in a young cheese. The card should state that and leave spoilage calls to the kitchen.
findings.fix: A firm, chalky center means it is young, and that is normal.

findings.claim: cow's milk, sometimes goat's milk, sometimes sheep's milk, sometimes added cream
findings.because: The rind is a surface-ripening Penicillium mold, grown on the cheese and eaten with it. Guests with a mold or penicillin concern often ask about it, but the one place ingredients act as warnings does not list it.
findings.fix: cow's milk, sometimes goat's milk, sometimes sheep's milk, sometimes added cream, white mold cultures

findings.claim: Confusion not linked from this side. Ghee (fd_0162) lists Brown Butter under confusedWithTerms and its notThis contrasts the two, but Brown Butter has Ghee only in seeAlsoTerms and no notThis. Both are butter whose solids toast, so a server who reads only this card cannot tell them apart.
findings.because: Confusion not linked from this side. Ghee (fd_0162) lists Brown Butter under confusedWithTerms and its notThis contrasts the two, but Brown Butter has Ghee only in seeAlsoTerms and no notThis. Both are butter whose solids toast, so a server who reads only this card cannot tell them apart.
findings.fix: Move Ghee from seeAlsoTerms to confusedWithTerms, keeping Meunière and Clarified Butter in seeAlsoTerms. Add notThis: "Not ghee, which toasts the solids and then strains them out. Brown butter keeps them in, and that is the flavor." The card is at 588 characters, so it has room.

findings.claim: The confusions are one-sided. Mascarpone (fd_0164) and Fromage Blanc (fd_0158) both list Ricotta under confusedWithTerms, but Ricotta lists neither as a confusion and has no notThis. Mascarpone even sits in its seeAlsoTerms. The origin ("the name means recooked") also repeats the first clause of the why word for word.
findings.because: The confusions are one-sided. Mascarpone (fd_0164) and Fromage Blanc (fd_0158) both list Ricotta under confusedWithTerms, but Ricotta lists neither as a confusion and has no notThis. Mascarpone even sits in its seeAlsoTerms. findings.fix: Set confusedWithTerms to ["Mascarpone", "Fromage Blanc"] and remove Mascarpone from seeAlsoTerms. Add notThis: "Not mascarpone, which is dense set cream, or fromage blanc, which is smooth and tangy. Ricotta is light, fluffy curds." Cut the origin to "Italy, a by-product of cheesemaking", or drop it, to pay for the notThis.

findings.claim: The confusion is one-sided. Chèvre (fd_0156) lists Feta under confusedWithTerms, but Feta has no confusedWithTerms and no notThis. Fresh goat cheese and feta get crumbled onto the same salads and are genuinely mixed up.
findings.because: The confusion is one-sided. Chèvre (fd_0156) lists Feta under confusedWithTerms, but Feta has no confusedWithTerms and no notThis. Fresh goat cheese and feta get crumbled onto the same salads and are genuinely mixed up.
findings.fix: Add confusedWithTerms ["Chèvre"] and notThis: "Not chèvre, which is soft, unbrined goat cheese. Feta is firmer, saltier and aged in brine." The card is at 606 characters, so it has room.

The why now says 'aged 12 months or far longer', so 36 months no longer reads as a ceiling.

The gist now says the solids are left in: 'Butter cooked until its milk solids toast, left in for a nutty taste'. The suggested wording used 'brown', which may not appear in this gist, so 'toast' is used instead. At 67 characters it stays within 5 of the trap.
The gist now marks this card off from Ghee: 'Mild, pale butterfat, most milk solids skimmed off before they brown'. The same change answers safety-12.
The guest line no longer claims house dishes. It now reads 'the classic secret to tender biscuits and juicy fried chicken'.
The guest line's second sentence now reads 'It's lovely with beets, honey or a warm salad.' It points at no dish on the menu and no longer echoes the Crème Fraîche line.
'Aged at least a year' is removed and the line now says 'hard, long-aged cheese'. 'Italian' is dropped as well, because a domestic parmesan need not be Italian, which is the point of the finding.
'Rich enough to boil' is replaced with plain words: 'Thick, mild cultured cream that won't curdle when hot'. It is kept at 53 characters so the gist is no longer than its 53-character trap.
The fragment is replaced with 'It's rich and warm.' and 'deeply savory' is dropped.

critic.notes: No card fails the build gate. The section mean is 634 characters of prose against the 720 ceiling. Every card is between 491 and 781 characters, and every field is inside its band. I found no verdict words, no em or en dashes, no banned substrings and no British spellings. No term, alias or listed word appears in a gist or trap. None of the roster rows carries a knownPacketError, so no trap is owed. Both accented terms (Chèvre, Crème Fraîche) have a say line, and every "say" follows the key. Pairs linked correctly in both directions: Burrata and Fresh Mozzarella, Bloomy Rind and Washed Rind, Clarified Butter and Ghee. The problems above are the three one-sided confusions and two length-parity cases. Minor points, not worth a gate: several madeWith lists leave out salt and rennet (Feta, Fresh Mozzarella, Burrata), and Brown Butter and Ghee have similar gists, though "left in" and "strained out" do tell them apart. I found no cross-section confusion missing: Brown Butter to Meunière and Compound Butter to Beurre Blanc are seeAlso links, which is correct.

findings.claim: Roccaverano is at least half goat
findings.because: The at-least-50-percent-goat rule is out of date. Regulation (EU) 2023/335 (1 February 2023) renamed the DOP 'Roccaverano' and now requires raw whole goat's milk only. Cow's and sheep's milk are no longer allowed.
findings.fix: Milk varies by maker: Roccaverano is all goat, Bosina is cow and sheep.

findings.claim: Robiola is milder and pale.
findings.because: This is too broad for a card whose origin names Lombardy. Lombard robiolas such as Robiola della Valsassina are washed-rind squares with a reddish rind. They are made like small Taleggios, so a guest who is served one would hear that it cannot look like this.
findings.fix: Not Taleggio, the square with an orange rind and loud smell. Most robiola is milder and pale.

findings.claim: often a blend of cow's, goat's and sheep's milk
findings.because: Three-milk robiola (tre latti) exists but is not the usual kind. Bosina uses two milks, Roccaverano uses goat only, and many robiolas are cow only. As written, the line leads a server to say three milks as the default.
findings.fix: often a blend of cow's milk with goat's or sheep's

findings.claim: Firm aged cheese shaved into thin ribbons over pasta and salads
findings.because: This trap is a true description of another roster card, Parmesan (fd_0159). A trap must not describe another card on the roster.
findings.fix: Aged stretched curd dried hard and grated over pasta and soup

findings.claim: burrata
findings.because: The Burrata entry is the long-form essay on burrata, the filled pouch. This card also lists Burrata as its main confusion (confusedWithTerms). Stracciatella only comes up in that essay's opening sentence, so the essay is not about the same subject.
findings.fix: omit lexiconSlug

findings.claim: Not Taleggio, the square with a sticky orange rind and loud smell. Robiola is milder and pale.
findings.because: Robiola is a family, as the card's own why says, and some of it is exactly that: Robiola Lombarda and Robiola di Valsassina are washed-rind squares with a reddish-orange rind. A flat 'Robiola is milder and pale' is false for those. The difference that holds on American menus (Bosina, La Tur, tre latte, Roccaverano) is that most robiola is smaller, paler and milder. 'Loud smell' is also slang a new hire should not repeat.
findings.fix: Not Taleggio, the big square with a sticky orange rind. Most robiola is paler and milder.

findings.claim: Also the name of a Roman egg soup and a gelato.
findings.because: The gelato is the stracciatella most American guests already know, and a server who reads 'a gelato' cannot tell a guest which one. It is the chocolate-chip one. Naming it is what lets a server clear up the confusion at the table. The shorter pouch clause makes room for it.
findings.fix: Not burrata, its pouch. Also a Roman egg soup and a chocolate-chip gelato.

findings.claim: strah-chah-TEL-lah
findings.because: The key asks for how an American dining room says the word, not the Italian double l. Americans reduce the unstressed vowels, and the sibling cards follow that pattern (boo-RAH-tuh, rih-KAH-tuh). A new hire reading 'TEL-lah' tends to stress the ending too.
findings.fix: strah-chuh-TEL-uh

findings.claim: roh-bee-OH-lah
findings.because: An American dining room reduces the final vowel, and the section's other Italian respellings end in -uh (boo-RAH-tuh, rih-KAH-tuh). This one should match.
findings.fix: roh-bee-OH-luh

findings.claim: Triple crème cheese, strawberries, honey, baguette
findings.because: No real menu or cheese list prints 'triple crème cheese'. The style word stands on its own, or follows a named cheese such as Brillat-Savarin. The added 'cheese' is what makes the line look written for a card.
findings.fix: Triple crème, strawberries, honey, warm baguette

findings.claim: It melts silky, hence pizza.
findings.because: This is clipped note-speak. It is not a sentence a new hire can take in or pass on when a guest asks why it is on the pizza.
findings.fix: It melts smoothly on pizza.

findings.claim: "cow's milk", "cream", "salt", "sometimes buffalo milk"
findings.because: Stracciatella is made from pasta filata mozzarella curd, and that curd is set with rennet, usually animal rennet. The other three cards in this section flag rennet (Triple Crème and Robiola list "often rennet", Taleggio lists "traditionally calf rennet"). Leaving it off this card only means a server checking the list for a guest who avoids animal rennet would find nothing to confirm with the kitchen.
findings.fix: "cow's milk", "cream", "salt", "often rennet", "sometimes buffalo milk"

findings.claim: The note is false. Robiola di Roccaverano DOP has to be at least 50 percent goat's milk, and the rest can be cow's or sheep's milk. So "Roccaverano is all goat" is wrong: only some Roccaverano is pure goat. The note also restates the madeWith list and the why ('often a blend', the Bosina example). It is not a doneness, raw-service or handling fact. At 752 characters this is the longest card in the section.

findings.claim: The two cards disagree about each other. Robiola (fd_0328) lists Taleggio under confusedWithTerms, but Taleggio lists Robiola under seeAlsoTerms. floor-deck.mjs symmetrises confusedWith, so the emitted Taleggio card ends up with Robiola in both confusedWith and seeAlso, which breaks the 'a term may not be in both' rule. critic.notes:
Checks that passed: all four todo rows (fd_0325 to fd_0328) have cards, and the 18 written rows already exist in tools/derive/floor-deck/dairy.mjs. The section mean with the four new cards as submitted is 656 characters, under the 720 ceiling. Every card is between 633 and 752 characters. I found no verdict words, no em or en dashes and no banned substrings. Every accented or hard term has a say. No row carries a knownPacketError. The gists and guest lines can all be told apart from their neighbours: Stracciatella and Burrata differ as the loose filling against the pouch. The one exception is Triple Crème against Bloomy Rind, which is raised above. The Stracciatella and Burrata link is one-sided, but floor-deck.mjs symmetrises confusedWith at build time, so Burrata's module needs no edit.

Facts checked: the triple crème grade is at least 75 percent fat in dry matter. Taleggio DOP ages at least 35 days, is washed weekly and uses calf rennet. Robiola Bosina is cow and sheep milk. Robiola di Roccaverano DOP is at least 50 percent goat, so the 'all goat' note is wrong. Source: https://www.piemonteagri.it/qualita/en/products/cheese/374-robiola-di-roccaverano-dop

Owner judgement calls, not gate failures:
(1) Stracciatella is placed at level 3 while Burrata is at level 2. Stracciatella is now common on good American menus and is the direct confusable of Burrata, so level 2 may fit the standard better.
(2) Robiola at level 4 is arguable. It shows up often on pizza and pasta menus, so level 3 may fit.
(3) Robiola's line 'Robiola agnolotti, brown butter, sage' nearly repeats Brown Butter's line 'Butternut squash agnolotti, brown butter, sage'. A different line, such as 'Robiola, truffle honey, focaccia', would read better across the deck.
(4) The Taleggio gist will sometimes be drawn as a wrong option on the Washed Rind question, and it describes one washed-rind cheese. It is specific enough (square, Lombardy) that I did not raise it as a problem, but a reconciler may want to watch it.

findings.claim: Goat cheese whose grey coat is a mold that must be cut away
findings.because: Half of this is true. On aged ash-ripened goat cheeses such as Selles-sur-Cher and Valençay, the grey-blue coat is partly mold (Penicillium, Geotrichum) growing over the ash. Only the 'must be cut away' part is false, and the trap's why ('The grey is plant ash dusted on by hand') is wrong for these cheeses, so a server who learns from it would tell a guest the grey-blue rind is only ash.
findings.fix: says: "Goat cheese whose grey coat is a burnt crust that must be cut away"; why: "The grey is plant ash dusted on before aging, and it is eaten with the rind."

findings.claim: often rennet
findings.because: The Époisses AOP rules require rennet. The curd sets mostly by slow lactic action, but a small dose of rennet is always added. 'Often' tells a guest who avoids animal rennet that some wheels might be made without it, and none are.
findings.fix: rennet

findings.claim: It tastes richer and more floral.
findings.because: The comparative has nothing to compare to: the guest's next question is 'richer than what?'. The point of the word is that it beats the same cheese made from valley or winter milk, so the line should say so in one breath.
findings.fix: The wheel was made up in a mountain hut in summer, from cows on alpine grass and flowers, so it's more floral than the valley version.

findings.claim: Confirm with the kitchen when a guest asks.
findings.because: This repeats the fixed sentence the app already adds after madeWith ('Confirm with the kitchen'). It sounds read off a card, and it costs characters without adding a fact.
findings.fix: Almost always made from raw, unpasteurized milk.

findings.claim: Goat cheese whose grey coat is a mold that must be cut away
findings.because: Half of this is true. On aged cheeses like Selles-sur-Cher and Valençay, the blue-grey coat is mold growing through the ash, so a server who knows the cheese could fairly pick it. The trap's why ('The grey is plant ash') leaves the mold out. Use a mistake that is wholly false.
findings.fix: Goat cheese rolled in cracked black pepper until its outside is grey

findings.claim: The grey is plant ash dusted on by hand, and it is edible with the rind.
findings.because: This has to match the replacement trap above, and it should not claim the whole grey coat is ash, because on aged cheeses part of it is mold.
findings.fix: No pepper: the grey is plant ash dusted on by hand, and it tastes of almost nothing.

findings.claim: Époisses, warm baguette, cornichons, Chablis
findings.because: Cornichons go with raclette and charcuterie, not with Époisses. The classic partners are bread and a white Burgundy such as Chablis, sometimes with walnuts. A new hire who learns this line will suggest the wrong garnish.
findings.fix: Époisses, warm baguette, walnuts, Chablis

findings.claim: The grey coat and any grey line through the middle are edible.
findings.because: "Edible" is a safety assurance a server will repeat as "it's safe to eat", and "any grey line" vouches for something the server cannot see. Loire ash cheeses such as Valençay and Selles-sur-Cher have no middle line. That line belongs to Humboldt Fog or Morbier. The real handling fact is missing: Valençay, Selles-sur-Cher and Sainte-Maure AOP must be made from raw goat's milk. Young cheeses sold in the US are pasteurized, because raw-milk cheese aged under 60 days cannot be sold there.
findings.fix: French originals are made from raw milk, most sold in the US are pasteurized. Confirm with the kitchen.

findings.claim: The grey is plant ash dusted on by hand, and it is edible with the rind.
findings.because: This is an edibility assurance inside a trap. It is also inaccurate: on an aged cheese the grey-blue coat is ash under a mold rind that grows through it, not ash alone.
findings.fix: The grey is plant ash under a thin mold rind, eaten with the cheese.

findings.claim: dusted with edible vegetable ash
findings.because: "Edible" in the guest line is a spoken safety assurance. Say what the ash is and leave out any word that vouches for it.
findings.fix: dusted with vegetable ash

findings.claim: dusted in edible charcoal
findings.because: "Edible" is an implied safety verdict, and the gist is shown as an answer that gets memorized and repeated.
findings.fix: dusted in vegetable charcoal

findings.claim: Ripe ones run, so it often comes in its wooden box with a spoon.
findings.because: The card says nothing about the milk, although this is the raw-service fact a server gets asked about. The Époisses AOP allows raw or pasteurized milk: the largest producer, Berthaut, pasteurizes and others make it from raw milk. Without this, the card says nothing either way, and a server may guess. A missing safety fact can lengthen the card.
findings.fix: Ripe ones run and come boxed with a spoon. Raw or pasteurized milk by producer, so confirm with the kitchen.

findings.claim: "cow's milk"
findings.because: Alpage cheeses are mostly cow's milk, but Swiss Alpkäse and some tommes d'alpage are made with goat's milk or a mix. A guest who reacts to goat's milk would not be warned.
findings.fix: "cow's milk", "sometimes goat's milk"

findings.claim: seeAlsoTerms includes Washed Rind. Ash-ripened goat cheeses grow a thin, wrinkled mold rind (the card's own why says so). They are never brine-washed. Linking Washed Rind points a new hire at the wrong rind family, and could become 'it's a washed-rind goat cheese' at the table.

critic.notes: The whole section has a card for every roster row: 22 already written in tools/derive/floor-deck/dairy.mjs, plus the three new ones, Alpage, Époisses and Ash-Ripened. Including the new three, the section mean is about 664 characters of prose per card, under the 720 ceiling. The new three come to 632, 740 and 747. No knownPacketError appears in this roster, so no trap is owed for one. I found no verdict language, no dashes and no banned substrings in the new cards, and none of their gists uses its own term or an alias. Gist and trap lengths are at parity: every trap is within 6 characters of its gist, and the gist is never the longest option. All three gists and guest lines are distinct from their neighbours (Washed Rind, Taleggio, Chèvre). Fact checks: the Valençay AOP specification requires raw, whole goat's milk (INAO cahier des charges), so the Ash-Ripened note holds; Époisses' minimum four weeks of washing with marc and its 1950s revival by Berthaut are correct; the 60-day rule makes US Époisses and young ash-ripened imports pasteurized. An optional cross-section link: Alpage (fd_0384) could take seeAlsoTerms ['Grass-Fed', 'Pasture-Raised'] from the language section, since the card's whole point is summer grass milk. Alpage also has no pairs line; origin is enough for context, but 'Quince paste, walnuts, Chasselas or Jura white' would help the second question. Small inconsistency on Alpage: the gist says 'from cows', while madeWith allows 'sometimes goat's milk'. That is acceptable but could be tightened to 'from herds on high pasture'.
